A S C L E P I V S.

for it shines through piety, religion, prudence, worship, and the veneration of God, as if seen with the eyes of true reason; and by the confidence of its own belief, it excels among men as much as the sun surpasses the other stars with its light. The sun itself illuminates the other stars not so much by the magnitude of its divine power as by its divinity and holiness. Believe, therefore, O Asclepius, that this is the second god, governing all things and illuminating all mundane beings, whether they are animate or inanimate. For if the world is a living creature, always having been, being, and destined to be, nothing in the world is mortal. Since every part of the living being, which is in the world itself—just as in one and the same ever-living animal—has no place for mortality, God himself must therefore be most full of life and eternity, if it is necessary for him always to live. The sun, therefore, just like the world, is everlasting; and thus it is the governor of vital things, or the constant companion and dispenser of all their vitality. God, therefore, is the everlasting governor of the living or vital things that are in the world, and the eternal dispenser of life itself. He has dispensed this once by an eternal law, providing life to all vital things in the manner which I shall now describe.

<summary>This passage defines the sun as a secondary god that acts as the eternal governor and dispenser of life to all beings within the living creature that is the world.</summary>
<keywords>Asclepius, the Sun, divinity, vitalism, eternity, governance of the world, secondary god</keywords>
